newsitem.title: USA: Democrats make gains in Washington state.
newsitem.headline: Democrats make gains in Washington state.

text.p: Washington state voters, who provided Republicans one of their biggest 1994 victories, sent at least one of six freshmen congressmen packing, while two other races were too close to call early Wednesday.
Democrats could win as many as five or as few as three of the state's nine seats in Congress, up from just two Democrats two years ago.

In the mostly suburban Ninth District south of Seattle, state Sen. Adam Smith defeated Randy Tate, the youngest memmber of the 1994 Republican freshman class, by a 53 to 47 percent margin with 73 percent of precincts reporting.

In another closely watched race in a suburban Seattle swing district, Republican Rick White kept his seat for a second term, narrowly defeating fellow-former prosecutor Jeff Coopersmith by 52 to 48 percent.

George Nethercutt, who toppled former House Speaker Tom Foley in 1994, easily beat wheat farmer Judy Olson in eastern Washington's vast Fifth District. And Republican Doc Hastings won a second term over Rick Locke in central Washington's Fourth District.

But Linda Smith, who had been pegged as a rising star in Speaker Newt Gingrich's congressional leadership, was losing to psychologist Brian Baird, who clung to a 3,000-vote lead. With 77 percent of the vote counted in southeast Washington's Third District, Baird had a 51 to 49 percent lead.
Smith, who made campaign finance reform her cornerstone issue, said she thought early returns broadcast from the East Coast might have discouraged some of her supporters from going to the polls.
And Jack Metcalf, the oldest member of the freshmen class, was losing to state Sen. Kevin Quigley, who had an even narrower 2,000-vote lead with half the votes counted.
Foley, analyzing the election for local televison, said he thought moderation had won out over the "extremism" of the 1994 vote that toppled him from office after 30 years in Congress.

"The public in this country and this region is very centrist in their political view of where the ountry should be going," he said. "Slow and steady is the motto. They don't want any party to do anything too fast or too rash."
